title: Given a Scenario, Configure Appropriate Scaling Approaches

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud workloads do not always need the same amount of resources. Demand may increase, decrease, follow predictable patterns, change suddenly, or respond to business events.
Scaling changes available resources so a workload can continue meeting demand efficiently.
CompTIA wants you to answer two different questions: when or why should scaling occur, and how should resources be scaled?
sections.callout: Scaling approach = when or why scaling happens. Scaling type = what gets changed.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: What causes the resource change, and should the environment add more instances or make existing instances larger?
sections.callout: The trigger determines when. Horizontal or vertical determines how.

entries.title: Triggered Scaling
paragraphs: Triggered scaling automatically changes resources when a defined condition occurs.
Instead of an administrator manually changing capacity, the environment responds to configured conditions.
Think: When this happens → scale.
entries.recognitionCue: If a condition automatically causes scaling → think triggered scaling.

entries.title: Scheduled Scaling
paragraphs: Scheduled scaling changes resources according to a predetermined time or schedule.
It works well when demand is predictable, such as increasing capacity before known business-hour traffic and reducing it afterward.
Think: We already know when the crowd is coming.
entries.recognitionCue: Predictable time-based resource change → scheduled scaling.

entries.title: Manual Scaling
paragraphs: Manual scaling requires an administrator to intentionally change resources.
It can fit rare scaling events, approval requirements, situations where automation is unnecessary, or environments requiring direct control.
Think: A human decides when to scale.
entries.recognitionCue: Administrator directly changes capacity → manual scaling.

table.caption: Scaling approach comparison
rows: A time or date causes scaling

entries.title: Trending
paragraphs: Trending uses observed patterns to determine that demand is moving toward a point where scaling is needed.
For example, traffic may increase steadily toward normal capacity, allowing scaling before the workload becomes overwhelmed.
Think: The numbers are heading this way.
entries.recognitionCue: Observed trend indicates a future capacity need → trending trigger.

entries.title: Load
paragraphs: Load-based scaling changes resources according to current workload utilization.
Indicators can include CPU, memory, request volume, or connection count.
Think: The system is busy right now.
entries.recognitionCue: Current workload utilization triggers scaling → load.

entries.title: Event
paragraphs: Event-based scaling occurs when a particular event happens, such as a message entering a queue, a file being uploaded, a job beginning, or an application event occurring.
Think: Something happened → scale resources.
entries.recognitionCue: A specific occurrence triggers scaling → event.

entries.title: Horizontal Scaling
paragraphs: Horizontal scaling increases or decreases the number of resource instances.
Instead of making one server dramatically larger, additional servers can share the workload.
Increasing instances is scaling out; reducing instances is scaling in.
Think: Add more machines.
entries.recognitionCue: Increase the number of instances → horizontal scaling.

entries.title: Vertical Scaling
paragraphs: Vertical scaling changes the capacity of an existing resource.
A virtual machine might grow from two CPUs and 4 GB of RAM to eight CPUs and 32 GB of RAM while remaining one virtual machine.
Increasing capacity is scaling up; reducing it is scaling down.
Think: Make the machine bigger.
entries.recognitionCue: Increase resources inside an existing instance → vertical scaling.

sections.title: Combining Scaling Concepts
paragraphs: A scenario can describe both an approach and a type because they answer different questions.
If CPU reaches 80% and the cloud platform automatically launches two additional instances, the approach is triggered scaling based on load and the type is horizontal scaling.
If an existing virtual machine is increased from four CPUs to eight every Monday morning, the approach is scheduled and the type is vertical.
sections.callout: Approach and type are not competing answers—they describe different parts of scaling.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: CPU or request utilization triggers scaling → Load
Scale at a predetermined time → Scheduled
Add CPU or RAM to an existing instance → Vertical

entries.title: Horizontal vs. Vertical
paragraphs: Horizontal means more machines. Vertical means a bigger machine.
Adding three instances is horizontal; increasing RAM from 8 GB to 32 GB is vertical.

entries.title: Triggered vs. Scheduled
paragraphs: Triggered scaling follows a condition or event. Scheduled scaling follows a clock or calendar.
If scaling is explicitly configured for 8:00 AM, it is scheduled even when the demand pattern is regular.

entries.title: Trending vs. Load
paragraphs: Trending uses an observed direction or pattern. Load uses actual current utilization.

entries.title: Event vs. Load
paragraphs: Event means something occurred. Load means resource usage reached a condition.

entries.title: Approach vs. Type
paragraphs: Do not confuse what caused scaling with what scaling changed. Ask both questions.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Make an existing instance bigger → Vertical
